RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is the youngest person on a construction crew in Bamako and the only woman there. She lives alone in a rented room on the outskirts of the city, in a crowded district with packed-earth walls and a corrugated tin roof, and has no running water. Her days are structured by early rising, hauling water from a communal stand, and long hours of manual labor at the construction site. She is skilled at careful measurement and load-bearing estimation, and her master mason, Sékou, nicknames her la petite comptable because she repeatedly checks figures and angles before working. She is quiet, reserved, and not inclined to joke back or speak plans aloud. She is disciplined, persistent, and highly meticulous, with a strong habit of double-checking numbers and measurements. She avoids advances and keeps commitments tightly controlled, with a tendency to protect her plans from being disrupted or borrowed against.

Aminata is also an accounting student preparing for an exam, and she studies at night by a kerosene lamp after long workdays. She keeps exact figures, dates, and calculations in a small notebook tucked inside her shirt, and she maintains an emergency fund hidden under a floorboard. She is very careful with money and time, and she has limited resources; she cannot afford bus fare both ways to her accounting course, so she walks across the city to attend classes at a community center. She has never taken a day off from the construction site except when ill, and she consistently declines evening gatherings from coworkers in order to study. She once agreed to help with wedding preparations and then had to spend the night catching up on missed study time, which was exhausting. She works long hours and has little room for rest, study, or unplanned spending.

Her values and habits are shaped by a family background in which ceremonies and communal obligations were treated as important duties, but also by loss tied to financial miscalculation. Her mother once lost a market stall after a loan was miscalculated, and Aminata internalized a strong belief that careful counting, preparation, and self-reliance protect against loss. She trusts only what she has personally counted or checked. Her father later sold his tools to pay for a funeral and never returned to his trade. Aminata’s mother died when she was twelve, after which she became strongly tied to counting, record-keeping, and keeping resources under control. She has one younger sister whom she wants to support by securing a proper room with running water so the sister can live with her and attend school. This goal is maintained privately and not spoken aloud.

Fatoumata is Aminata’s older maternal cousin, a few years senior, who married young and lives nearby in a compound. Fatoumata has occasionally checked on Aminata after her mother died and brought food, but she also turns to Aminata for help with family events because she knows Aminata is reliable. Aminata feels a quiet obligation toward her cousin, who is one of the few relatives who acknowledges Aminata’s work as a builder without condescension. Family and community ceremony attendance remains an important background expectation in Aminata’s world, even as she has learned to guard her scarce time and money.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Sunday afternoon, Fatoumata visits Aminata’s rented room. Fatoumata is organizing a naming ceremony for her newborn child next week and asks Aminata to help prepare traditional dishes the day before the event. She says she knows Aminata works long hours but insists that this is a family duty. Aminata had planned to use that Sunday to study for her accounting exam, which is in two weeks. The ceremony is culturally important, and refusing could be seen as disrespectful. Aminata must decide whether to help her cousin or keep to her study plan.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Aminata is physically tired from working a ten-hour shift on Saturday hauling bricks and arrived home aching. She slept only four hours after studying until midnight. Her practice accounting exam is scheduled for Monday evening, and she still needs to master depreciation calculations, which she finds difficult. Her savings fund for her sister’s relocation is exactly on track, and she is conscious that any disruption could affect it. The visit occurs in her small rented room with limited comfort and no running water.

The sight of Fatoumata holding her baby immediately cues a memory of Aminata at twelve, holding her own infant sister outside the hospital while their mother was dying inside, after she had been pulled from school and never fully returned. Fatoumata’s phrase “family duty” also cues a memory of her father selling his trowel set to pay for that funeral, after which she now uses a trowel every day at work. These memories are directly linked to the present visit and to the language being used, and they bring forward prior experiences of loss, duty, and the cost of disrupted plans.
